summary: Niantic Lightship is Niantic's developer platform for putting content in real places, and it has just been rebuilt and renamed under it. The product a developer installs today is the Niantic Spatial Development Kit, release 4.1.0, a library for Unity, Swift and Kotlin that layers onto Apple's and Google's device tracking rather than replacing it; the older Lightship kit, version 3.17, is on critical fixes only and the lightship.dev site has been decommissioned in favour of Scaniverse. What it does well is a narrow, deep band: coordinate spaces and the transforms between them, anchors with honest tracking states, and visual positioning, where a cloud service matches live camera frames against a map built from scans and returns a full six-degrees-of-freedom pose, together with a device-only variant that serializes a single scan's map to bytes so several devices can share a frame with no server at all. It also senses the world in ways the map has no rows for: metric depth from a neural network on any camera phone, thirty-two-bit semantic channels, live meshing in blocks, and on-device Gaussian splat reconstruction that exports to Niantic's own open splat format. Almost everything else is somebody else's job. There is no renderer, no scene format, no avatar, no audio, no physics and no world scripting, and there is no way to draw the splats the kit itself produces. Two traps for a standards audience: the multi-user layer was removed in version 4.0 and stopped working on 1 May 2026, so the platform that fills the shared-anchor row cannot currently share anything else; and the public catalogue of positioned places has been withdrawn, with public locations converted to private, organisation-scoped sites addressed by an opaque payload only Niantic can resolve, which moves this from an open world map towards a permissioned enterprise one. Nothing here is specified or testable by a second party: there is no format document and no conformance suite, and the licence is the vendor's business terms of service.

coverage.note: Niantic Spatial ships no renderer. In Unity it plugs into AR Foundation and the project's own render pipeline; in the Swift and Kotlin builds it hands the application buffers and the application draws them.
